title: The Athari approach
hookLine: a man asks Imam Malik how Allah rose over the Throne, and gets an answer in four parts

cards: Medina. Imam Malik is sitting with his students when a man comes up and asks about a verse. The Qur'an says Allah rose over the Throne.
How did He rise? The reports say Malik lowered his head for a long moment, and he began to sweat. Then he looked up and answered.
The rising is known. The how of it is beyond grasping. Believing in it is a duty.
And asking about the how is an innovation. Then, in the version people repeat, he had the man shown out.

teach.b: Here's the verse, in Pickthall's translation: "The Beneficent One, Who is established on the Throne."
The Athari approach takes its name from athar, a report or a trace: the narrations handed down from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions. Its method is simple to say.
When the Qur'an or an authentic hadith describes Allah, with a hand, a face, rising over the Throne, coming, laughing, affirm it as it came. Don't explain it away as a figure of speech.
Don't picture it like a human body.
And don't ask how: in Arabic, bila kayf, without how.

teach.h: PASS IT ON AS IT CAME.
teach.b: A saying reported from several early scholars puts it in one line: pass these texts on as they came.
Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who stood through the trial, is remembered as holding this way, and the approach has been tied with the Hanbali school since; later, Ibn Taymiyya defended it at length.
Notice the difference from the last few days. The Mu'tazilah reasoned their way to a created Qur'an. Al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi built careful arguments to defend tradition.
The Atharis were often wary of kalam itself, not because they disliked thinking, but because they believed some questions about Allah are not ours to answer, and that the words He chose are enough.

There's a discipline in that: letting a verse about God stand, without filling the gap with pictures. Ash'aris and Maturidis also used this restraint at times. The schools argue about when to use it, and how far.

how: Muslims who follow the Athari approach, often associated with the Hanbali school, affirm the descriptions of Allah in the Qur'an and authentic hadith as they came, without likening Him to creation and without asking how (bila kayf).

o: the old Arabic poetry the early scholars used to explain verses
a school that relies on reason alone, apart from the reports
affirming what Allah says of Himself as it came, without asking how

games.q: the Athari approach — tap the pairs.
p: the rising is known, the how is not

s: Atharis say Allah has a body like ours
they affirm the texts without likening Him to anything created.
Atharis explain away the verses as figures of speech
they affirm them as they came and leave the how to Allah.

games.q: you're Imam Malik. a man asks you how Allah rose over the Throne. what do you say?
o: say the verse doesn't really mean rising.
the rising is known, the how is not; belief is a duty, asking how is an innovation.
games.why: the reports say Malik lowered his head and sweated before giving that answer, and had the questioner shown out.

practice: Say the verse slowly, aloud or in your head: The Beneficent One, Who is established on the Throne.

Each time your mind reaches for a picture, a chair, a sky, a king, set it down gently, the way Malik set down the question, and keep only the words. If you'd rather, rest on the two words without how.

wordCard.voice: The Athari approach. The way of the early reports: affirm what Allah says of Himself, as it came, without likening and without asking how. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: without how; affirming without asking the manner.

carryVoice: Your line: as it came. The words are let stand, without a picture. Rest well.
